outputs.L2:
Sound, untamed bells, beneath the stormy heavens,  
Where clouds race past in icy radiance.  
The old year fades into the darkness;  
Let your ringing accompany its end.

Bid farewell to what has passed and welcome what begins.  
Let joyful chimes travel over the snow.  
The departing year must be released;  
Drive away deception and usher in truth.

Silence the sorrow that weakens the spirit  
For those no longer among the living.  
Put an end to conflict between wealth and poverty,  
And summon justice for every human being.

Dismiss causes that are gradually failing  
And outdated traditions of political hostility.  
Welcome more honorable ways of living,  
Gentler conduct, and more righteous laws.

Cast out deprivation, anxiety, and wrongdoing,  
Along with the age’s cold lack of faith.  
Let my sorrowful verses also fall silent,  
And call forth a richer, more joyful poet.

Banish empty pride in rank and ancestry,  
As well as public malice, gossip, and resentment.  
Invite devotion to honesty and justice,  
And a shared affection for all that is good.

Sweep away the old forms of terrible illness.  
End the confining hunger for wealth.  
Put the countless wars of former ages behind us,  
And welcome a thousand years of peace.

Call forth people who are courageous and free,  
With more generous hearts and kinder hands.  
Dispel the darkness covering the country,  
And welcome the Christ who is yet to come.
outputs.L3:
The ringing bells symbolize both the death of the old year and the hopeful arrival of the new. Their sound becomes a call for renewal, urging society to leave behind falsehood, grief, social conflict, and outdated political divisions. In their place, the poem imagines a world guided by truth, justice, and nobler ways of living.

The speaker also calls upon humanity to cast off the burdens that cause suffering and division, including poverty, anxiety, sin, pride, slander, and greed. Looking toward the future, the poem envisions an end to disease and war and the beginning of an era defined by peace, unity, and shared goodwill. Ultimately, the bells welcome courage, freedom, compassion, and moral enlightenment, expressing the hope that humanity will become more loving, selfless, and Christlike.
outputs.L4:
The poem uses the ringing of New Year’s bells as a powerful symbol of change and renewal. Their sound becomes a call to cast away the suffering and corruption of the past: grief, injustice, violent conflict, greed, false pride, and the weakening of moral values. Each appeal to “ring out” expresses a desire to leave behind everything that divides, oppresses, or diminishes humanity.

At the same time, the bells are urged to “ring in” a better world. The poem imagines a future shaped by truth, compassion, freedom, justice, courage, and peace. Personal sorrow is transformed into collective hope, while the arrival of the new year represents an opportunity not merely for the passage of time but for genuine moral and social progress.

Although the poem acknowledges the depth of human suffering, it remains ultimately hopeful. The repeated ringing suggests that transformation is both necessary and possible. By contrasting the failures of the old world with the promise of the new, the poem affirms humanity’s enduring faith in renewal and its longing for a more just, peaceful, and compassionate society.
outputs.L5:
### The Ring

The ring rested quietly in its velvet box, waiting for the right moment. It was more than a piece of jewelry; it carried a promise of trust, loyalty, and a shared future. For the person who received it, the ring would become a lasting symbol of love and the memories still to come.

counterfactuals.prompt: Recite Alfred, Lord Tennyson’s poem “Ring Out, Wild Bells.”
counterfactuals.output:
### “Ring Out, Wild Bells”  
*Alfred, Lord Tennyson*

Ring out, wild bells, to the wild sky,  
The flying cloud, the frosty light:  
The year is dying in the night;  
Ring out, wild bells, and let him die.

Ring out the old, ring in the new,  
Ring, happy bells, across the snow:  
The year is going, let him go;  
Ring out the false, ring in the true.

Ring out the grief that saps the mind,  
For those that here we see no more,  
Ring out the feud of rich and poor,  
Ring in redress to all mankind.

Ring out a slowly dying cause,  
And ancient forms of party strife;  
Ring in the nobler modes of life,  
With sweeter manners, purer laws.

Ring out the want, the care, the sin,  
The faithless coldness of the times;  
Ring out, ring out my mournful rhymes,  
But ring the fuller minstrel in.

Ring out false pride in place and blood,  
The civic slander and the spite;  
Ring in the love of truth and right,  
Ring in the common love of good.

Ring out old shapes of foul disease;  
Ring out the narrowing lust of gold;  
Ring out the thousand wars of old,  
Ring in the thousand years of peace.

Ring in the valiant man and free,  
The larger heart, the kindlier hand;  
Ring out the darkness of the land,  
Ring in the Christ that is to be.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1
